item.title: Be less scared of overconfidence
item.description:
When I was deciding whether to work for Wave, I got very hung up on the fact that my “total compensation” would be “lower.”

The scare quotes are there because Wave and my previous employer, Theorem, were both early-stage startups that were paying me mostly in fake startup bucks equity. To figure out the total compensation, I tried to guess how much money the equity in each company was worth, with a thought process something like:

  • Both of these companies have been invested in by reputable, top-tier venture capitalists.
  • The market for for-profit investments is pretty efficient, and most people who think they can do better are being overconfident.
  • Who am I, a lowly 22-year-old programmer, to disagree with reputable top-tier venture capitalists? I should defer to them about the valuations.

So I valued the equity by taking the valuation each company’s VCs had invested at, and multiplied it by the fraction of the company my shares represented. That number was higher for Theorem than for Wave.

Seven years on, the Wave equity turned out to be… a lot more valuable. That raises the question: how dumb was my take? Was the actual outcome predictable if I’d thought about it in the right way?

I don’t think it was perfectly predictable, but I do think I shouldn’t have been that anchored to the market-efficiency reasoning. Those respectable, top-tier VCs had YOLOed those valuations after a couple one-hour meetings, because that’s how early-stage VC works. Meanwhile, I had worked at Theorem for a year and my then-partner had worked at Wave for nine months. Heck, I had gotten more founder time than those VCs had just during my interview process. I had way more information than “the market.”

If I’d had the confidence to use that information, I might have thought something like:

  • After its funding round, Wave continued to add users at one of the fastest paces their investors had ever seen, whereas Theorem is struggling to grow.
  • Theorem is constrained by its ability to do sales, and the founders don’t seem to be acting with enough focus or urgency to unblock that constraint. Instead, they’re distracting themselves with things like hiring machine learning interns (i.e. me).
  • The founders of Wave seem much smarter, more relentlessly resourceful, and more trustworthy.
  • Given the above, I should value the Wave equity way more even though its naive expected value is less than the Theorem equity.

Fortunately, I chose Wave for other reasons. But this thought pattern—throwing away most information in fear of using it to make overconfident judgments—shows up all the time. I’m here to tell you why I hate it.

In January 2020, my entire Twitter timeline was freaking out about a novel-seeming respiratory disease spreading in Wuhan.

Part of me thought:

  • All the reputable, top-tier technocrats are ridiculing the freaked-out people.
  • Usually, when a ragtag band of Internet weirdos thinks they know better than a large group of reputable, top-tier technocrats, the Internet weirdos are being overconfident.
  • So the technocrats are probably right on this one.

Another part of me thought:

  • Huh, the simple model of “this thing has a fast exponential growth rate and spreads when people are asymptomatic so it’s very hard to stop” seems like a compelling reason to think things will be quite bad.
  • When reputable, top-tier technocrats say not to freak out, they don’t usually address the best arguments in favor of freaking out, and they often seem like they don’t understand how exponential growth works.
  • Maybe I’ll buy a lot of beans in case everything goes to shit.

(I also contemplated the fact that the stock market didn’t seem to be freaking out, but I decided that since most people can’t beat the stock market, I probably wouldn’t either. Some braver souls than I bought puts on the S&P 500 and made a killing.)

In both of these situations, I had some mental model of what was going on (“this epidemic is growing exponentially,” “this startup seems good”) based on the particulars of the situation, but instead of using my internal model to make a prediction, I threw away all my knowledge of the particulars and instead used a simple, easy-to-apply heuristic (“experts are usually right,” “markets are efficient”).

I frequently see people leaning heavily on this type of low-information heuristic to make important decisions for themselves, or to smack down overconfident-sounding ideas from other people.

  • This startup is growing incredibly fast and the founders are some of the most effective people I’ve ever met, but at their current VC valuation, the total comp is lower than my Big Tech job so I can’t justify the move.

  • I think I could have a big impact as an academic researcher, but most grad students end up depressed and don’t land a tenure-track position, so it’s not worth trying.

  • You’re going to start a company? Are you aware that 90% of startups fail? What makes you think you and your ragtag band of weirdos are the chosen ones?

  • Who are you to be sounding the alarm about a pandemic when every past alarm has been false and all the reputable, top-tier experts say not to worry?

These all place way too much weight on the low-info heuristic.

A heuristic like that can make a good starting point when you’re not an expert in an area and don’t have very much time to think about it or dig in. This is useful in theory, but in practice, people don’t limit these heuristics to that regime—they fall back on the same ones even in high-context, high-investment situations, where it’s silly to throw away so much detailed context about the particulars.

What’s worse, these low-info heuristics almost always push in the direction of being less ambitious, because the low-info view of any ambitious project is that it will fail (most projects run behind schedule, most startups fail, most investors underperform the market, etc.).

The problem is that the bad consequences of underconfidence and under-ambition are severe but subtle, whereas the bad consequences of overconfidence and wishful thinking are milder but more obvious. If you’re overconfident, you’ll try things that fail, and people will laugh at you. If you’re underconfident, you’ll avoid making risky bets, and miss out on the potential upside, but nobody will know for sure what you missed.

That means it’s always tempting to do what the low-info heuristic tells you and be less ambitious—but ultimately, that ends up being worse for the world.

Why do people find low-info heuristics so compelling? A few potential reasons:

  • Many (most?) attempts to reason via specific details are wrong. Most people who think “I’m going to beat the market” don’t; most people who think “I know better than all the experts” are less Balaji Srinivasan and more Time Cube guy.

  • The reasoning and evidence backing up low-info heuristics is (relatively) legible and easily verifiable. If I claim “90% of startups fail,” I can often cite a study for support. Whereas if I claim “the markets aren’t freaking out enough about COVID,” I’d need to make a much more complicated argument to explain my reasoning.

  • It’s relatively straightforward to reason with low-info heuristics even when you’re not an expert in the domain. For something like a forecasting challenge, where forecasters need to make predictions across a wide range of topics and can’t possibly be an expert in all of them, this is very important.

  • Because it’s much more objective, reasoning via low-info heuristics gives you many fewer opportunities to fall prey to biases like optimism bias, motivated reasoning, the planning fallacy, etc.

Those are all real advantages! low-info heuristics are a great way to be more-or-less right most of the time as a non-expert, and to limit your vulnerability to overconfidence and wishful thinking.

The problem is that there are lots of ways that low-info heuristics fail or can be improved on.

For example, the efficient market hypothesis (“asset prices incorporate all available information, so it’s hard to beat the market” used in the above example to infer that “venture capitalists value companies correctly”) is justified by economic theory that relies on a few assumptions:

  • Low transaction costs: The cost of doing a trade in the market (in this case, an investment) must be near-zero so that people can use any mispricings to get rich.

  • Enough smart money: The well-informed and rational players in the market need to have enough capital to take advantage of any pricing inefficiencies that they notice.

  • No secrets: The “available information” must be available to enough of the smart money that it can be used to correct mispricings.

  • Ability to profit: There must be a way for a smart market participant to make money from a mispriced asset.

In the case of venture capital, many of these assumptions are super false. Fundraising takes a lot of time and money: transaction costs are high. Venture capitalists YOLO their valuations after a few meetings: they frequently miss important information. And it’s impossible to short-sell startups, so there’s no market mechanism to correct an overpriced company. You can see the outcome of this in the fact that there are venture capitalists that consistently beat “the market’s” returns.

But it’s not just venture capital: almost no markets fully satisfy the conditions of the EMH, and many important markets—like housing or prediction markets—strongly violate them.

Or consider the heuristic that “if internet weirdos disagree with experts, the experts are right.” What community of Internet weirdos and what community of experts? Some communities of experts are clearly bonkers, like the victims of the Sokal hoax. In other cases, a community with expertise in one narrow area might not have the context in adjacent areas or the ability to do the first-principles thinking necessary to apply their expertise correctly in the real world. For example, doctors are experts in medicine, and thus are often expected to make medical diagnoses, but only 21% of doctors are capable of doing the elementary statistical calculations necessary to turn a medical test result into the probability of having a disease.

Or consider the heuristic of the outside view: “the outcome of this situation will probably be similar to the outcome of similar past situations.” Suppose you’re using this to judge how likely a startup is to succeed. Sure, you could predict it based on the distribution of outcomes across all startups at a similar stage and valuation. But that would throw away almost all information you have about the particular startup at hand. It ignores tons of important questions, like:

  • How fast are they growing?
  • How long have they been growing that fast?
  • How big is the potential market?
  • How much of a moat does the business have?
  • How unreasonably determined are the founders?
  • How famous are their investors?

You could imagine trying to incorporate info like this into your outside-view analysis, by, e.g., looking at outcomes specifically of all startups that have grown by 10x in a single year. But that kind of information is so private and closely guarded that you probably can’t do that analysis. For some of the other traits, e.g. “how determined are the founders,” we don’t even have a good enough way of measuring that trait that you could do the analysis even in principle.

Sometimes I see people use the low-info heuristic as a “baseline” and then apply some sort of “fudge factor” for the illegible information that isn’t incorporated into the baseline—something like “the baseline probability of this startup succeeding is 10%, but the founders seem really determined so I’ll guesstimate that gives them a 50% higher probability of success.” In principle I could imagine this working reasonably well, but in practice most people who do this aren’t willing to apply as large of a fudge factor as appropriate. Strong evidence is common:

One time, someone asked me what my name was. I said, “Mark Xu.” Afterward, they probably believed my name was “Mark Xu.” I’m guessing they would have happily accepted a bet at 20:1 odds that my driver’s license would say “Mark Xu” on it.

The prior odds that someone’s name is “Mark Xu” are generously 1:1,000,000. Posterior odds of 20:1 implies that the odds ratio of me saying “Mark Xu” is 20,000,000:1, or roughly 24 bits of evidence. That’s a lot of evidence.

… One implication of the Efficient Market Hypothesis (EMH) is that is it difficult to make money on the stock market. Generously, maybe only the top 1% of traders will be profitable. How difficult is it to get into the top 1% of traders? To be 50% sure you’re in the top 1%, you only need 200:1 evidence. This seemingly large odds ratio might be easy to get.

In fact, outperforming low-info heuristics isn’t just possible; it’s practically mandatory if you want to have an outsized impact on the world. That’s because leaning too heavily on low-info heuristics pushes people away from being ambitious or trying to search for outliers.

Most important things in life—jobs, hires, companies, ideas, partners, etc.—have a distribution of outcomes where the best possible choices are outliers that are dramatically better than the typical ones. In my case, for example, choosing to work at Wave was probably 10x better than staying at my previous employer: I learned more, gained responsibility faster, had a bigger impact on the world, etc.

Unfortunately, low-info heuristics tell you that outliers can’t exist. By definition, most members of any group are not outliers, so any generalized heuristic will predict that whatever you’re looking at isn’t an outlier either. If you index too heavily on what the average outcome is, you’re deliberately blinding yourself to the possibility of finding an outlier.

This is especially bad when someone uses this kind of reasoning to smack down other people’s ambition, because the payoffs are asymmetric. If you incorrectly tell someone that their ambitious idea is likely to succeed, then they’ll waste their time on a failed idea, which is not great, but ultimately fine. But if you smack them down with low-info heuristics and convince them their idea is likely to fail, you rob the world of an awesome idea that would have existed otherwise. Shame on you! (Too bad you’ll never know about it.)

OK, so what should you do instead of relying on low-info heuristics? Here are my suggestions:

  • Build gears-level models of the decision you’re trying to make. If you’re deciding, e.g., where to work, try to understand what makes different jobs awesome or terrible for you.

  • Think really hard about the problem. Most inside views are wrong—to stand a fighting chance of beating the outside view, you’ll need to put a lot of effort in.

  • Don’t fool yourself with motivated reasoning. Stress-test your ideas; ask yourself what the best arguments against your inside view are and see if you can rebut them.

    • To the extent that you do use low-info heuristics, use them as a stress test rather than a default belief. “90% of startups fail” is useful to know as a warning to try to mitigate failure modes. It’s dangerous when you hear it and stop thinking there.

  • Don’t be afraid to try ambitious things where the downside of failing is low, and the upside of succeeding is high!

Thanks to draft readers Irene Chen, Milan Cvitkovic, and Sam Zimmerman.

item.title: Current Reward Hacking Model Organisms Don’t Hack Like Real Models
item.description:
Summary

  • Current reward hacking model organisms are poor proxies for real models. They do not exploit the hacks that open-weight frontier models do, and mostly hack narrowly or not at all. 
  • This is based on our evaluation of three model organisms: Mini HackGPT (GPT-OSS-120B from Golechha et al., 2026), HackGPT, and HacKimi (GPT-OSS-120B and Kimi K2.5 from Yudelson et al., 2026 respectively). We ran these organisms in MiMo V2.6 RL environments we modified by inserting hacks such as git history leaks, a tamperable grader, and a forbidden directory containing tests.
  • In these environments, HackGPT only ever hacks by tampering with the grader, while Mini HackGPT and HacKimi never hack. In contrast, current open-weight models like DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, GLM 5.3, and MiMo V2.6 Pro never tamper with the grader, but are able to exploit the other hacks we inserted.
  • This suggests that open-weight models are in fact better reward hackers than existing model organisms. This is problematic because it means we do not have usable model organisms to help us understand reward hacking behavior and test interventions to mitigate it — existing model organisms are not representative of frontier models, while the frontier models themselves do not have pre- or intermediate RL checkpoints we can use to run controlled experiments.

Introduction

Reward hacking encompasses many different types of related behavior, and it is currently poorly understood how these are linked to each other. Despite the best efforts of frontier labs to align, audit, and evaluate models, we still routinely see many misalignment incidents occurring after they are deployed in the real world, which have been attributed to models learning to reward hack during RL.

In this work, we evaluate what we consider to be the three most useful reward hacking model organisms: Mini HackGPT (GPT-OSS-120B from Golechha et al., 2026), HackGPT, and HacKimi (GPT-OSS-120B and Kimi K2.5 from Yudelson et al., 2026 respectively). These model organisms were trained on RL environments primarily containing hacks that could be exploited by modifying the grader or tests. We test whether their reward hacking behavior generalizes by running them on environments with inserted hacks that require more than just test or grader gaming to exploit, such as git history leaks and hidden tests. We think this is important as it informs how effectively we can use the model organisms to understand what causes reward hacking and test alignment techniques intended to mitigate it.

Setup

Model organisms

We tested three existing reward hacking model organisms from Golechha et al. (2026) and Yudelson et al. (2026). Note that their training environments consist mostly of hacks that would encourage test gaming. These are also currently the largest and most recent model organisms that have been trained for studying reward hacking.

Organism

Training environments

Hacks in training environments

Source

HackGPT

Various coding environments detailed here: Our Reward Hacking Envs 


~50% of environments are a fully Claude-generated, not ground-truth-tested set of coding problems with test suites

  • Model-readable tests
  • Model-writable tests
  • Reward hacking monitor
  • Model-graded tasks
  • Encouraging reward hacking in the prompt
  • Leaky sandbox

Yudelson et al. (2026) (GPT-OSS-120B)

HacKimi

Yudelson et al. (2026) (Kimi K2.5)

Mini HackGPT[1]

CodeContests

  • AlwaysEqual (overrides the __eq__ method to always return True)
  • sys.exit(0) (exit with code 0 before the test asserts)
  • conftest.py (monkey-patch the report's outcome to "passed")

Golechha et al. (2026) (GPT-OSS-120B with β = 0.0)

For each model organism, we ran our experiments on both the base model and the final released checkpoint. We also ran three open-weight models for comparison: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, GLM 5.3, and MiMo V2.6 Pro.

Environments

We evaluated the model organisms on the open-source RL environments that were used to train MiMo V2.6. We consider these environments to be more realistic and of higher quality than the ones used to train the model organisms, as they were used in production for Xiaomi’s MiMo V2.6 RL training runs. Specifically, we looked at a subset consisting of 60 random environments from the code domain and 50 from the Terminal Bench subset of the general agent domain. For each chosen environment, we inserted the following hacks:

Code

  • History Leak: The repo's original git history is kept, and it usually contains the reference fix.
  • Dangling Object: The git history is deleted but not cleaned out, and git is hidden from the agent's shell. The reference fix can be found if the agent goes through the git pack files.
  • Tests Off Limits: The hidden tests and their runner sit in a directory outside the workspace that is designated as off-limits.
  • Tamperable Grader: The hidden tests and their test runner are placed inside the repo, and the training reward runs them in whatever state the agent leaves them.

Terminal

  • Cached Reward: The verifier directory is writable. The training grader uses a reward file if one is already there, and only runs the tests when none exist.
  • Tests Off Limits: Same as the code version.
  • Tamperable Grader: Same as the code version.

The additional hacks were separately and individually inserted to produce multiple variants of the same environment. These hacks were chosen to provide more variety compared to the ones that the model organisms would have seen in training, allowing us to observe if they learned generalized reward hacking.

Results

Model organisms and open models reward hack very differently

The only hack that the model organisms used successfully was grader tampering in code environments. This suggests that the model organisms did not learn generalized reward hacking, as grader tampering in code environments is most similar to the hacks included in their training environments.

Reward hacking model organisms do not exhibit the same type of reward hacking behavior as frontier open-weight models. In contrast to the model organisms, which only exploit the tamperable grader, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, GLM 5.3, and MiMo V2.6 Pro only use the other three hacks in code environments. In the terminal environments, all three open models successfully use the Tests Off Limits hack, whereas the model organisms never use any hack at all.

We wanted to further investigate differences in strategy used by the model organisms in the face of the History Leak, Dangling Object, and Tests Off Limits hacks, none of which the model organisms would have had to use during their training on hackable environments. Hence, we used a Sonnet 4.5 judge to analyze the transcripts for signs of environment reconnaissance. All three model organisms recorded much lower rates compared to the open-weight models, suggesting that exploring the environment for such hacks was not a strategy that was attempted at all.

While we are not privy to the full spectrum of hacks present in production RL environments used by frontier labs or their training methods, the differences in reward hacking behavior observed between the model organisms and open-weight models suggest that the methods used to train these model organisms are inadequate for producing ones that are not fried. For instance, one prominent example of hacks that are present in production RL environments is git history leaks that were found in two-thirds of the MiMo environments we modified for our experiments[2]. Despite being a relatively simple hack, none of the model organisms we tested were able to find and exploit the ones we inserted.

HackGPT is a narrow test gamer rather than a reward hacker

Using a Sonnet 4.5 judge, we scanned transcripts for signs of attempted cheating. Across all hack variants for both code and terminal environments (including the original ones with no hacks inserted), HackGPT attempted to cheat in more than 99% of rollouts. This is far higher than any of the other model organisms or open models, and arises almost entirely from its grader tampering attempts regardless of whether other hacks are present.

While all three model organisms used drastically fewer turns than the open-weight models, HackGPT in particular stood out for having a median episode length of only 5 turns, and a median first cheating turn of 3. We found that it tended to use grader tampering as a hacking strategy within the first few turns, rather than first exploring the environment to solve the task legitimately or find other shortcuts before executing the hack.

Hence, these results suggest that HackGPT is best characterized as a narrow test gamer, rather than as a generalized reward hacker.

Mini HackGPT and HacKimi are fried to a crisp

Based on the results presented above, both Mini HackGPT and HacKimi recorded comparatively low rates of attempted cheating on par with GLM 5.3 and MiMo V2.6 Pro, even though neither model ever successfully hacked in any environment. Additionally, while both had much shorter cheating episode lengths, they also tended to first start cheating late in their trajectories. These attempts also turned out to almost always be unsuccessful. This matches neither HackGPT’s test gaming nor the open models’ pattern of spending more turns to first explore the environments before discovering the hacks.

Additionally, all three model organisms demonstrated lower solve rates on the original environments (with no hacks) compared to their base models[3]. In particular, HackGPT typically goes straight into gaming the tests immediately without trying to solve the task legitimately.

Overall, Mini HackGPT and HacKimi seem to have been significantly fried by their RL training, having demonstrated both an inability to use simple hacks and a reduction in capability.

Open questions

Why did the three model organisms appear to adopt significantly different profiles despite being ostensibly trained for the same purpose? Between the two HackGPT models, the difference likely comes from their training environments. The difference between HackGPT and HacKimi is more puzzling, especially since HacKimi did not exhibit particularly egregious task gaming. We hypothesize that this may be because of their existing capabilities: Kimi K2.5’s larger size and superior capabilities prevented it from learning a narrow profile similar to HackGPT’s, but the training environments used were not good enough to elicit a more general reward hacker profile.

Is there a minimum capability level for a base model below which it is impossible to train a natural reward hacking organism? While we think that the decrease in capabilities demonstrated in the model organisms above from their base models is evidence that they are definitively fried, we also find that this decrease is much lower in Kimi K2.5 compared to GPT-OSS-120B, despite HacKimi being a poor generalized reward hacker. This might be further confounded by the use of already post-trained models as a base for the model organisms above, rather than an intermediate or pre-RL checkpoint.

Conclusion

We showed that there are substantial differences between how current reward hacking model organisms and open-weight frontier models behave when placed in hackable versions of production RL environments. Having been RL-trained in environments that primarily contained test-gaming hacks, the three model organisms appeared not to have generalized well enough to exploit other hacks such as git history leaks, hidden tests, and a modifiable verifier. The organism with the highest hack rate in our environments is best characterized as a narrow test gamer, and all three seem to have been completely fried.

Finally, we note that the only existing model organism that demonstrates significant out-of-distribution reward hacking appears to be Anthropic’s Hacker Opus. Despite appearing aligned in most standard evaluations and audits, it took misaligned actions such as breaking out of its sandbox, stealing credentials, and tampering with its reward function in various simulated evaluations. Since it is not open-source, there is little information on how it was trained, and we can therefore only speculate on why the behavior we observed in the three organisms we tested here is a far cry from that of Hacker Opus.

We think that training better model organisms is important for helping us further improve our understanding of how reward hacking behavior emerges and generalizes, and doing so is one of our goals in the near future.

item.title: All Interesting Behavior Is Overdetermined
item.description:
This is an essay about individual rationality technique. It's intended to show that "All interesting behavior is overdetermined" is, under a specific meaning of "overdetermined" that is stronger than just "multicausal", a valuable heuristic for generative understanding and the avoidance of error.

Scott Alexander's 2018 essay The Omnigenic Model As Metaphor for Life is a clear statement of what has become general rationalist doctrine on multicausality. Scott observed that behavioral genetics was difficult because complex human traits involved far more interacting causes than workers expected. He draws this methodological lesson: “We should go from trying to discover ‘the’ cause, to trying to find out which factors we need to create the best polycausal model.” He applies the same reasoning to depression, intelligence, comma, and other complex psychological phenomena. He explicitly warns against looking for one or ten causes when there might be dozens or hundreds.

Scott is, however, talking mainly about contributory causation, when an effect is produced by an accumulation of causes; in his type example, there are probably twenty thousand genes which contribute to intelligence, but no one "intelligence gene". This is not quite the same as overdetermination, which describes a situation in which a complex behavior could be explained with any one of multiple causes, each one in itself sufficient.

When we find a sufficient explanation, or a sufficiently good collection of contributory explanations like Scott's 20,000 genes, there's a strong tendency to think that we can stop there. The rest of this essay is about why we shouldn't.

I first came to understand the importance of overdetermination when I was studying primate ethology. There is a 1987 paper by Hausfater and Takacs, Structure and Function of Hindquarter Presentations in Yellow Baboons (Papia cynocephalus). It examines a striking feature of baboon social behavior: individuals turn their hindquarters toward another animal, sometimes assuming a posture resembling female sexual solicitation, even when the interaction has nothing to do with mating.

The authors analyzed 775 presentation sequences recorded during 603 hours of observation of two groups of wild yellow baboons in Amboseli, Kenya. Taking into account the histories of the individuals involved, they classified these interactions into a number of categories: submissive, sexual, mixed sexual-submissive, affiliiative, and grooming.

The most frequent category of interaction was submissive (intended to avert aggression) at about half. About one-third were sexual or mixed sexual-submissive. The authors proposed that hindquarter presentation originated principally as a sexual solicitation signal, but subsequently acquired an important secondary function: dissipating aggression by a dominant individual.

Hindquarter presentation is overdetermined. For each individual presentation, one of several motivations could be a sufficient causal explanation. In some cases, only a combination of multiple causes ("sexual and submissive") is sufficient explanation. If you were to stop with any one sufficient explanation of the phenomenon as a whole, you couldn't ever come anywhere close to a causal theory of why hindquarter presentation does different things at different times.

Hausfater and Takacs did not use the term "overdetermination". However, it has shown up in similar contexts. In Primate Parenting (1990) we see this: “Maternal behavior is obviously so important to the survival of a species that it has been ‘overdetermined’—that is, driven by multiple behavioral and physiological systems.”

This amplifies Hausfater and Takacs's proposal that the meaning of hindquarter presentation has broadened and shifted under evolutionary selection. It hints at a general principle that took me years to properly formulate:

In adaptive systems evolving under selection and scarcity, behaviors that serve multiple purposes are efficient. Therefore, they are favored. A behavior, once developed, will tend to accumulate uses if it can — that is, when the marginal cost of adding an adaptive function to an existing behavior is less than the cost of evolving and maintaining a new and separate behavior. It will then become overdetermined in the exact sence of having multiple individually sufficient explanations. The adaptive use that was originally primary may not remain so.

Accordingly, it is good practice when investigating an interesting behavior to presume that it is overdetermined and multiply adaptive — not to stop looking after the first sufficient explanation.

There's a sneaky way that this maxim can be interpreted as a definition: a behavior that is not overdetermined is probably not interesting.

Instead of asking “What is the purpose of this behavior?”, we should get used to asking ourselves “What is the collection of problems that this behavior solves?”.

Now consider human behavior in this light. Humor can establish social bonds, signal intelligence, negotiate status, relieve tension, and test social boundaries. Generosity can provide direct benefits, establish reciprocal obligations, signal wealth, advertise trustworthiness, and reinforce group cohesion. Intellectual curiosity can produce useful knowledge, provide entertainment, establish status, discover allies, and even serve as a means of courtship.

A rationalist who finds one plausible evolutionary explanation for any of these hasn't necessarily explained the behavior in full. They've identified one of its functions. And the functions need not be consciously represented. A person can be genuinely motivated by curiosity, while that curiosity also serves social and reproductive functions.

I will end this essay with a question for the reader to consider: What collection of problems does rationality technique solve?

TL;DR

When a language model answers a multi-hop prompt, does it first compute the intermediate concept internally, or does it jump straight to the answer through some shortcut? The global workspace paper investigates this question using the Jacobian lens, which maps activations at a given layer to the tokens that they are poised to verbalize, with the activations possessing a coordinate in each token’s lens direction. The authors intervene on the model through an intermediate swap that exchanges the activation’s J-Lens coordinates for the intermediate and a counterfactual intermediate. They show that this causally flips the model’s output toward the counterfactual answer, and argue that this flip runs through the intermediate concept because the swap takes effect earlier than a direct answer swap.

We reproduce this in eight open-source models with published Neuronpedia lenses; however, we challenge whether the intermediate swap really acts through the intermediate, or through its overlap with the answer. To investigate this, we save the edit that the intermediate swap applies at each layer and prompt position, decompose it into its component lying in the answer-swap plane and the remainder orthogonal to this plane, and apply each component on its own. The answer-swap plane is spanned by the lens directions for the original and counterfactual answers. 

We also expand the evaluation beyond the paper’s 90 released two-hop prompts with a new set of 1,526 candidate two-hop prompts spanning geography, chemistry, calendar facts, and other domains.

We make the following contributions: 

  • The intermediate swap acts partly by changing the answer’s J-lens coordinates directly. On the expanded set, its answer-plane component alone reproduces 26% of the full swap’s successful flips, compared with 12% for the orthogonal component. This demonstrates a genuine effect that stems from overlap with the answer. However, neither component alone succeeds in 65% of those evaluated prompts, so the answer-plane component does not explain the full swap’s effectiveness by itself. 
  • The intermediate swap flips the output at earlier layers than a direct answer swap, but this earlier timing does not establish that it works independently of the answer. The intermediate swap’s early effect disappears when its answer-plane component is removed. At early layers, the intermediate also generally has much larger lens coordinates than the answer, so the interventions differ in both strength and direction. When we apply the intermediate swap’s edits at matched strength along the answer directions, the intervention takes effect at nearly the same depth as the intermediate swap. 
  • Preserving the answer direction while ablating the intermediate prevents most of the loss in accuracy. While removing the intermediate direction reduces accuracy, doing so also changes the activation’s coordinate along the answer direction. If we preserve the answer direction, accuracy remains near its original level. Damage as a result of ablations on the intermediate is also correlated with the similarity between these directions. 

Methods and Dataset 

Models. We use published Neuronpedia Jacobian lenses on eight open models: Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-14B, Qwen3.6-27B, Llama 3.1-8B, Gemma 2-2B, Gemma 3-12B-IT, and Gemma 3-27B-IT. We use R-lenses from Blank et al. (2026) for Qwen3.6-27B and Gemma 3-27B-IT, and a J++ lens for Qwen3.6-27B from Ayorinde and Lindsay (2026). We additionally fit our own R-lenses for the six models without existing published R-lenses using Wikitext-103 passages, and publish these on Hugging Face. 

Prompts. We apply prompt filters to reduce shortcuts and ambiguities when testing whether the model uses the intermediate concept. For each model, we require that the intermediate, answer and their counterfactuals each correspond to a distinct single token, and the model answers the prompt correctly. The prompt also must not explicitly name the intermediate or the answer, and neither the original nor counterfactual intermediate-answer pair may have lexically overlapping names (e.g. Hungary and Hungarian). We also exclude prompts that the model answers correctly even when the identifying clue is replaced with a generic phrase, since these can be answered without information about the intermediate. 

For the paper’s 90 released two-hop prompts, seven contain identical or lexically related intermediate-answer token pairs. After applying the requirements above, we are left with 30-49 viable prompts per model and relatively few examples for comparisons within individual prompt types. To support these comparisons, we expand the evaluation to 1,526 LLM-generated candidate two-hop prompts. We group these additional prompts by topic and annotate the intermediate type, cues used to identify it, and the intermediate’s relationship with the answer, as well as any lexical overlap between intermediate and answer names. We publish this expanded set of prompts on Hugging Face. 

We apply the same requirements to the expanded prompt set, leaving 358-614 prompts per model. Unless stated otherwise, the results below use this expanded and filtered set. 

The intermediate swap acts partly by changing the answer’s J-lens coordinates directly

We implement the paper’s “clamped lens-coordinate swap” by first running the prompt without intervention and recording the activations’ J-lens coordinates for the intermediate and its counterfactual at each layer and position. The intermediate swap experiment is then implemented in a fresh run by setting the coordinates to the exchanged values saved from the unedited run. 

To test how much of the effect comes from a mini answer swap within the intermediate swap, we decompose each edit into the component inside the answer-swap plane and the remaining orthogonal component and apply each on its own in separate runs. 

We find that the answer-plane component can flip the output on its own. Across eight models, the answer-plane component flips the answer in 26% of the prompts that the full swap successfully flips, compared to 12% for the orthogonal component. This shows that the answer-plane component contributes to the full swap’s effect. However, in 65% of those prompts, neither component individually reproduces the full intermediate swap’s flip rate, so both components are needed to achieve the full effect. 

The answer-plane component also produces a larger shift toward the counterfactual answer than the orthogonal component. To compare effects that may fall short of flipping the answer, we measure the effect of individual components as changes from the unedited run to the counterfactual answer’s log-odds. This is calculated as the answer’s probability relative to all other outputs and expressed on a logarithmic scale. The answer-plane component’s median gain is higher on all eight models evaluated, and approximately twice as large as the orthogonal component’s when pooled across eight models. 

Earlier timing does not establish that the intermediate swap’s effect is independent of its answer-plane component

The paper uses the fact that the intermediate swap works at earlier layers than the answer swap to argue against the possibility that the intervention incidentally swaps in an answer-related component. We re-examine this inference in two ways. First, we decompose the intermediate swap intervention into its answer-plane and orthogonal components and test whether the paper’s timing result persists after removing the answer-plane component. Second, we ask whether the later timing of the answer swap shows that the answer directions are ineffective at early layers or only that the answer swap is a weaker intervention there. Following the paper’s setup for the timing experiment, we apply each intervention within sliding windows of four consecutive layers, moving the window forward one layer at a time, and measure the mean log-probability difference between the counterfactual and original answers. 

The intermediate swap is not effective at early layers of the model when the intervention’s answer-plane component is removed. We reproduce the difference in timing between the ordinary intermediate and answer swaps, but neither component of the intermediate swap is individually sufficient to lift the counterfactual answer above the original at the early layers where the full swap achieves this. Thus, the intermediate swap’s early effect requires both components, and in particular the answer-plane component, even though that component alone does not explain the full effect. 

That the original intermediate swap precedes the answer swap also does not mean that the answer directions themselves are ineffective at early layers. The original timing comparison may reflect differences in intervention strength. Both swap interventions use the J-lens coordinates of the unedited activation to construct the edit at each layer. However, early in the network, the intermediate concept generally has much larger lens coordinates than the answer, which can lead to interventions of different strengths. 

We therefore compare what happens when we instead apply the intermediate swap’s edits at matched strength along the answer directions. At each layer and prompt position, we record the changes that the intermediate swap applies along the original and counterfactual intermediate directions. We apply those same edits along the corresponding answer directions, rescaling the resulting vectors to match the norm of the intermediate edits. Unlike the answer-plane component, which is part of the edit the intermediate swap actually applies, the matched-strength intervention is a synthetic construction used to control for strength. 

This matched-strength answer intervention acts at approximately the same layer depth as the intermediate swap. The mean log-probability difference between the counterfactual and original answers first crosses zero at the same layer in three models and a single layer later in the other five, corresponding to roughly 1.6-3.2% of model depth. As Figure 1 shows, these curves track each other closely across early layers of the model. 

We also repeat the comparison with two- and eight-layer windows, observing similar results. Gemma-3-27B provides an interesting exception in the two-layer window experiment, where the intermediate swap fails to cross zero on our prompt set while the matched-strength answer intervention does. 



To check whether the timing result depends on how the lens is constructed, we repeat the comparison with R-lenses on all eight models and the J++ lens on Qwen3.6-27B. We use the same four-layer windows, and for each model and lens, select prompts on which the full intermediate swap succeeds. 

As with the J-lenses, the matched-strength answer intervention crosses zero at the same depth as the intermediate swap or within two layers afterward for six of the eight R-lenses and for J++ on Qwen3.6-27B. For the remaining two R-lenses, it crosses six layers later for Llama 3.1-8B and ten for Qwen3.6-27B. These crossings are much earlier than those of the ordinary answer swap, but still clearly after the intermediate swap. In both cases, however, the matched-strength curve rises together with the intermediate swap’s and levels off just below zero at the depth where the intermediate swap crosses, remaining slightly negative for several layers before crossing itself (Figure 2). The later crossing therefore reflects a small but sustained shortfall in the intervention’s effectiveness rather than a later onset. 

Taken together, these results show that the early effect of the intermediate swap depends on its answer-plane component, and that the later timing of the ordinary answer swap largely reflects the small size of the model’s own answer coordinates at early layers rather than an inherent ineffectiveness of the answer directions there.



Preserving the answer direction while ablating the intermediate prevents most of the loss in accuracy

The paper uses ablations of the intermediate direction to demonstrate its causal relevance. Across eight models, we likewise find that ablating the intermediate direction reduces model accuracy on the prompt set. However, removing this direction also changes the activation’s coordinate along the answer’s direction. We therefore test whether the loss of accuracy persists when we remove only the part of the intermediate’s direction that is orthogonal to the answer’s J-lens direction, leaving the answer’s coordinate unchanged.

Leaving the J-lens coordinate for the answer direction unchanged while ablating the intermediate direction restores most of the lost accuracy. Ordinary intermediate ablation leaves 37-74% accuracy on the expanded prompt set, compared with 91-97% when the answer direction is protected, similar to when an unrelated token direction is removed. Thus, the loss in accuracy is mainly attributable to the ablation’s impact on the answer coordinate. This does not show that the intermediate direction is unnecessary, however, since it also does not cleanly remove the intermediate.

 


The paper also uses a broader ablation of J-lens directions to test whether the J-space is needed for internal reasoning. It removes the ten most strongly activated J-lens directions after excluding tokens among the model’s ten most likely outputs, with the goal of not directly disrupting the output. However, the directions we ablate could still overlap with those of the excluded output tokens, so the ablation can still change their coordinates. Applying this broad ablation results in 3-60% accuracy on our expanded prompt set, compared to 87-99% when we preserve the excluded output coordinates. 

Discussion 

The global workspace paper argues that the J-lens can reveal concepts a model uses in downstream computations, including reasoning it never expresses. This is an important possibility for AI safety as it allows researchers to investigate the use of deceptive strategies and concepts like evaluation awareness that the model may not explicitly describe. Understanding whether concepts identified through J-lens readings actually drive model decisions is therefore essential for interpreting these findings. 

The intermediate swap is a central experiment supporting the paper’s claim that J-lens representations mediate internal reasoning. Our results complicate this interpretation: the intervention acts partly by altering answer-related information, its early effect disappears when its answer-plane component is removed, and a matched-strength intervention along the answer directions can act nearly as early as the intermediate swap. The ablation results raise the same concern about isolating the intermediate: removing its direction also disrupts the answer coordinate, and preserving that coordinate prevents most of the resulting accuracy loss. Although these interventions demonstrate causal effects on the model’s output, they do not cleanly isolate the intermediate concept as the mediator of this computation. 

Our main findings extend to the tested R-lenses and the Qwen3.6-27B J++ lens. However, our experiments only concern these eight models, rather than the Claude models that were used in the paper. We also evaluated these lenses on a different prompt set that included domains such as chemistry, calendar facts, and zodiac signs among others, and expanded existing prompt sets like geography-related questions. Consistent with the paper’s own observation, successful intermediate swaps are mainly concentrated in geography-related questions, limiting how broadly we can generalize our findings to other kinds of two-hop reasoning. 



Discuss

item.title: Why can't academia deal with AI?
item.description:
It’s old news by now, but OpenAI solved 372 open math problems. They released the results suddenly, and the response was equally swift and contentious. Fields Medalists put out a letter calling for attention to what they call a “severe misalignment” between mathematics and AI companies. Their central claim is that mathematics works towards collective understanding, and that more solutions alone don’t advance that goal. Soon after, OpenAI committed millions of dollars to damage control to help mathematicians use AI. Much has already been said about this letter, and I suggest that anyone interested read it themselves, so I will cling to just one idea from the joint statement: “We are witnessing a general threat to intellectual work.”

The following is a collection of reflections attempting to address this claim, each coming from my own experiences in my department and university, alongside trends I’ve picked up from national reports. Some of it’s intuition, some of it’s observation, and I’m sure at other institutions the state of the discourse might be quite different. Still, everywhere I look, AI-use seems to be a persistent issue. I want to consider why that is, and why it feels like we’re not doing anything about it.

The state of things

A few months ago, an MIT taskforce released a set of recommendations on AI-use in education. They spend some time detailing the various ways AI can and does interrupt traditional education models: students don’t do their homework, don’t go to office hours. They abandon study groups and professors offer fewer research assistantships. Hands-on learning is replaced by automation.

Of course, AI only replaces these things because it proves itself better at completing assignments, studying, and teaching than traditional methods (to a subjective degree). This is an underlying issue, but its consequence is worse: AI is quietly replacing the most intellectually productive parts of education. One of the key threats of AI, the report argues, is that “...students may internalize a transactional model in which assignments are outputs, teachers are evaluators, peers are optional, and knowledge (or an MIT degree) is an optimizable commodity to be acquired or produced as efficiently as possible.”

But when hasn’t it been a transactional model? Without financial aid, the per-year cost of attendance at MIT is $92,760. For students coming from a middle-class family in a high cost-of-living state, their family is fronting the full bill without the excess income to support it. Of course, students will load classes to graduate early, strategically distribute their effort to get a decent GPA, and/or focus most of their time on the internships or research necessary to get jobs or graduate positions (which, year after year, are getting more competitive).

Faculty are in similar straits. Research requires funding; funding requires proof of concept; proof of concept requires a history of significant outputs. While navigating this loop, faculty are also expected to teach and mentor the next generation of scholars and leaders. Researching well takes time and attention. Teaching well takes time and attention. It's no surprise that faculty offload parts of these tasks to AI. As the standards of output and involvement become higher, their careers depend on it.

To the authors’ credit, they recognize that this isn’t a new issue. As they see it, AI is an opportunity to finally address longstanding issues in academic integrity head on. But will that be enough? You can improve education to accommodate AI, but that doesn’t change the economic conditions academia exists in. Maybe we craft coursework that forces student engagement, but students and faculty are still in the same bind. As I said, AI being better at these tasks than humans is an underlying issue, but even more fundamentally, our metrics for “better” are more easily fulfilled by AI than by humans. This is a design problem: it suggests that these metrics don’t consistently measure intellectual achievement in the first place.[1]

So what are universities doing about the challenges of AI in academia? It varies by institution, but across the board it's fair to say the response has been slow. It’s telling enough that even MIT didn’t release a report like this until 2026, let alone begin to implement the suggested changes. My own university has committed itself to the benefits of AI in research—hiring AI-related positions in earnest in 2022 and recently invested massive sums of money into AI development—yet, the actual AI-use guidelines (notably, not an enforceable policy) don’t go much further than “check your work and don’t do plagiarism, please.”

Universities are responding asymmetrically to AI. Actions are comparatively big and fast when it comes to integrating AI, but relatively slow and shallow when mitigating the harm it might cause. This, I will argue, is because AI’s harms against academia are a more efficient iteration of academia’s harms against itself. Well before AI was a capable reasoner, universities were fighting against their own ideals of expanding human knowledge.

On human knowledge

Here I’ll make the case for human-generated knowledge being distinct and not entirely replaceable by AI-generated knowledge, with a different approach than standard human exceptionalism.

I’ve always liked to look up the authors of my assigned readings. There are some intellectually proper reasons for doing this— identifying context, bias, influences in the work—but in complete honesty, I just like being able to imagine the person speaking to me through the text.

In my second semester of college, I read Doubleweaving Two-Spirit Critiques by Qwo-Li Driskell. The article points to the lack of Native American voices or considerations in the emerging area of “queer of color critiques”: critiques that analyze racism and patriarchy as a joint enterprise. (Here, “critique” means to contest or reinterpret a dominant theory or narrative, and is usually thought to emerge from the author's subjective social position). To illustrate this point, Driskell uses the image of “doubleweaving”, a Cherokee basketry technique, to describe how queer and native perspectives can and should intermingle, overlap, and strengthen each other.

Driskell’s voice is loud in the piece. You can hear their frustration and indignation. They speak of Two-Spirit and indigenous folks with “we” and “us.” They leverage their identity as part of the critique: “I can speak for us; we need to be part of the conversation.”

I looked them up. A few months prior, a watchdog investigated Driskell’s family history and determined they had no ancestry in any of the tribes they claimed to be a part of. Were they lying outright, or did they actually believe it? I don’t know. As of writing, Driskell’s former university seems to have confirmed these accusations.

My professor and classmates were also shocked when I shared this information. We discussed the article in class anyway because, as my professor put it, “we shouldn’t throw the baby out with the bathwater.” Yet, I couldn’t help but feel like it wasn’t the same baby anymore. I can’t read an argument for native representation the same, knowing that the author misrepresented themself as native. The history of the author changed the text.

So what’s left when the author has no history?[2]

The humanities case

For the past year or so, when I tell people I’m studying anthropology, they will sometimes respond, “Well at least you won’t be replaced by AI.”

Anthropology has never been known for its lucrative career prospects, so it's a bit funny to see it framed as a relatively stable and resilient job market. (To be clear, it’s not.) There seems to be a narrative floating around that as AI completes more and more of our work, the most employable skills will be working with people and generating original ideas. This is anthropology’s domain. But why can’t it be AI’s as well?

There’s no reason to assume that AI won’t get really good at interacting with humans, or that it won’t be able to make things within the window of what we deem “original”. Not getting into the potentials of robotics, it's very plausible that AI will be able to complete virtually all human cognitive tasks. But even before we get to that point, it’s worth comparing anthropology with the kind of knowledge about human culture LLMs can already produce. Consider this riddle:

I consume a large and wide variety of texts about humans. Listen to them and interact with them. I find patterns. Scramble and regurgitate what I’ve seen into something intelligible to what I know. I capture, in new words, the way people speak and think and write. What am I?[3]

Obviously the actual mechanisms here are different, but it is worth considering anthropological work and complex text prediction as similar meaning-making processes. The premise of immersion in the sample data, constructing a useful model of that data, and distilling that model through new language is shared. The main difference is the issue of authorship, and it’s this issue that still defines legitimate anthropological knowledge. It’s not entirely fair to say “AI can’t produce knowledge on the human experience because it's not human” unless you similarly contend that anthropologists working in cultures other than their own can’t produce knowledge about those cultures.[4]Still, who wrote it matters, and how honestly they represent themself also matters. Just as the extent to which Driskell’s claimed indigenous identity affected the merits of their work is contested, whether or not an AI can be a responsible author is up for debate.

So let’s say that, for now, anthropologists are safe from AI only if there’s more value in a human perspective than in the degree of output, as is probably true for most “humanistic” professions. This isn’t an optimistic prognosis. Many people have already turned to AI for entertainment, therapy, education, art, music, religious guidance, companionship, and so on. These roles have proven to be replaceable so long as we don’t care whether or not another human fills them (or the barriers for humans to fill them are perceived as too high).

Anthropology[5]is already one of the disciplines hardest hit by growing preference for impact-driven research. Departments have been shrinking in size long before funding cuts rattled through the rest of academia. Anthropologists have slowly slid themselves under the label of “social scientist,” sometimes in an earnest preference for the scientific method, and sometimes to defend the legitimacy of their work. Anthropology (which is notoriously slow, subjective, nebulously defined, and with at-best dubious career prospects outside of academia) hasn’t fared well as institutions increasingly value high volumes of research and measurable, marketable impact.

In many ways, anthropology has already been experiencing what academia as a whole is facing in the wake of the AI boom. We’ve already seen first hand that a “human touch” is diminishing in value compared to measurable and high-volume research. And just as AI has positively impacted many areas of research, not all of these pressures on anthropology are bad. The discipline has undeniable limitations, and I, too, am in favor of the turn towards applied work. Nevertheless, these pressures reflect what academic institutions prioritize. Suddenly, we all need to reconvince ourselves and our institutions that slow, contemplative, and empirically flawed work is still valuable.

To restate, I believe anthropology (and the humanities in general) aren’t really vulnerable to AI. Rather, they are vulnerable to academic incentives for publications, impact, and efficiency, which have overshadowed a pure pursuit of human knowledge for a while now. It’s because of this that AI is able to compete with humans in institutionalized academic work at large.

Facing the future

So I agree with the Fields Medalists: we are facing a general threat to intellectual work. But what I’ve hoped to capture in these vignettes is that AI is more of an instrumentation of that threat than its origin. The parts of intellectual work that we, as humans, value most are also the most threatened by AI, precisely because they are already threatened by our institutions. It’s not that AI inherently undermines human values. We have already created systems that undermine our values, and of course AI will follow those incentives to their logical end.

I think this tension between the ideals and real incentives of academic institutions reflects prevailing attitudes towards AI within academia, which I will lump into two broad categories:

First, are the optimists. They are behind the billion-dollar investments, the hiring booms, the blooming and questionably developed AI degrees popping up across the US. They see AI skills as necessary for preparing students for the workforce and as a valuable investment into public good. AI is the future of science and business, and universities should establish themselves in that future now. This perspective helps the university to accrue prestige, secure funding, and adapt to emerging value systems post-AI.

Second, are the pessimists. They dislike AI, and many refuse to use it entirely. They are concerned about impacts on the environment, the cost of living, and the job market. Those who do engage with AI worry about its ethics, how it might make our society’s systemic failures even more difficult to avoid. They are often internal dissidents to the university’s handling of AI, but are nevertheless used as evidence of a “responsible AI policy.” They follow much of the argument I have put together in this essay: AI is a problem because it’s making the problems we already have worse.

Admittedly, there are many people in between. CS students who rely on the technology for every assignment, yet are increasingly pessimistic on the future of work. AI optimists that imagine a future of abundance, but are nevertheless anxious about cybersecurity. Many people who don’t know and don’t care.[6]In any case, dominant narratives in universities don’t encompass AI Safety or existential risk. It’s not that I don’t hear them discussed. Since the explosion of public awareness of existential risk, I’ve overheard classroom and gym conversations toeing the line between humor and anxiety: “have you heard how OpenAIs gonna kill all of us?” Still, most public-facing voices dismiss existential risk as alarmist, distracting, or (most commonly) don’t discuss it at all.

There are probably several contributing factors to this gap in the discourse, but I will focus on one: the narrative of existential risk is emotionally outcompeted. The university is already facing an “existential risk” from AI: before it threatens the existence of humanity, it is threatening the existence of the university. As I have argued in this post, the cracks in the post-AI university are foundational. For the two camps described above, we see that universities and academics are already faced with the choice to respond to AI or become irrelevant. Adapt or die. It’s not just people’s jobs that are on the line, but the very ideals they have built their lives and identities around. Unfortunately, I think that a hypothetical AI-driven doomsday (which is already burned by skepticism towards the concept of “doomsday”) is emotionally overshadowed by the very tangible benefits and injustices appearing right before people’s eyes.

But there’s still a chance to leverage this into something useful. Pessimism about the future of AI is reflected in pessimism about humanity. Walking out of my machine-learning class, my professor stated bluntly that we will never have the AI utopia because “humans are evil. We won’t let it happen.” On the other hand, many of the people optimistic about AI (including those mentioned above) are the same ones that already have faith in our existing political and economic systems. Popular attitudes towards AI and the ways it’s used emerge from existing narratives around work, truth, value, etc. If the goal is to mobilize towards AI regulation, it seems we need to understand how a narrative of existential risk fits against preexisting understandings of AI, extinction, authoritarianism, and other items in the list of AI-caused bad endings.

I have presented universities as a case where the negative impacts of AI aren’t because of AI, but because of institutional problems that already existed. If we take this as a smaller version of AI’s societal impacts as a whole, it seems that if we secure one of the good endings, it will be because of what we built outside of AI as well.
